overview: Dermatologists are physicians who treat conditions of the skin, hair and nails, from acne and eczema to skin cancer. They perform full skin exams, take biopsies, remove lesions and offer cosmetic procedures. O*NET rates knowledge of medicine at 4.82 out of 5 for this job and customer service at 4.58, since many patients return for years. The path is long: medical school, then a residency in dermatology, which is among the most competitive specialties. The BLS May 2025 median is $328,730 across 11,370 jobs. Hours are often predictable, and many dermatologists run their own practices.
pay: Dermatologists earn a median of $328,730, and the top 10% earn $578,560 or more. Minnesota has the highest state median at $625,790, 90% above the national figure. New York has the most dermatologists, 2,070, with a median of $374,010. Pay depends heavily on practice ownership and cosmetic work.

faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $328,730 a year. The middle half earn between $139,990 and $452,450, a wide range that reflects practice type and location. Minnesota, Washington ($526,170) and New Hampshire ($516,230) have the highest state medians, while Connecticut has the lowest at $165,040.

faq.q: How long does it take to become a dermatologist?
faq.a: It usually takes 4 years of college, 4 years of medical school and a residency of about 4 years, including an intern year. In O*NET data, 56% of dermatologists hold a doctoral degree and 31% report post-doctoral training. Board certification follows residency.

Less than many physicians. In O*NET data the job ranks above 97% of U.S. jobs for keeping the same hours every week, and above 99% for freedom to make decisions. Clinic schedules are mostly daytime, though exposure to infection and being on your feet are common.

O*NET rates critical thinking at 4.12 out of 5 for this job and active listening at 4. A steady hand matters for biopsies and surgery, and knowledge of administration and management, rated 3.87, helps dermatologists who run their own practices and staff.
